thread.title: DHS Reviewing Plan to Transform Warehouses into Detention Facilities
thread.title_full: DHS Reviewing Plan to Transform Warehouses into Detention Facilities

author: HEATHER HOLLINGSWORTH
title: DHS Reviewing Plan to Transform Warehouses into Detention Facilities
text:
• Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is reviewing a plan to transform warehouses across the U.S. into detention facilities.
• Immigration officials have spent $1.074 billion on 11 warehouses.
• The Department of Homeland Security paused the purchase of new warehouses after Mullin was sworn in.
• The department is scrutinizing contracts signed under former Secretary Kristi Noem.
• A 418,000-square-foot warehouse in Surprise, Arizona, was purchased for $70 million.
• A contract worth at least $313.4 million was awarded to transform the Surprise warehouse.
• DHS is now planning to start with 250 people per week and cap occupied beds at 542 in Surprise.
• A 439,945-square-foot warehouse in Orlando, Florida, was toured by private contractors and federal officials.
• ICE bought a warehouse in Social Circle, Georgia, for $128.6 million, with plans to house 7,500 to 10,000 detainees.
• The city of Social Circle is concerned about water supply and put a lock on the warehouse's water meter.
• DHS bought a 540,408-square-foot warehouse in Oakwood, Georgia, for $68.2 million.
• A warehouse in Merrillville, Indiana, was toured by ICE, but the owner stated no negotiations were ongoing.
• ICE purchased a warehouse in Washington County, Maryland, for $102.4 million, with a renovation contract worth at least $113 million, but work is on hold due to a lawsuit.
• A 250,000-square-foot warehouse in Romulus, Michigan, was purchased for $34.7 million, and the state and city sued.
• Owners of warehouses in Woodbury and Shakopee, Minnesota, pulled out of potential deals after public outcry.
• A possible detention center in Byhalia, Mississippi, was opposed by local officials, and Noem agreed to look elsewhere.
• A warehouse sale in Kansas City was canceled after public pressure.
• DHS will not move forward with a proposed ICE facility in Merrimack, New Hampshire.
• DHS bought a 470,044-square-foot warehouse in Roxbury, New Jersey, for $129.3 million, and the township and state sued.
• ICE announced the purchase of a warehouse in Chester, New York, but later said it was no longer considering the facility.
• Property owners in Oklahoma City informed the mayor they are no longer engaged with DHS.
• DHS purchased warehouses in Tremont Township and Upper Bern Township, Pennsylvania.
• ICE mistakenly announced the purchase of a warehouse in Lebanon, Tennessee, and the deal was later canceled.
• ICE paid $122.8 million for three warehouses in Socorro, Texas, and $66.1 million for a warehouse in San Antonio.
• A real estate company in Hutchins, Texas, confirmed it was contacted but would not sell or lease to DHS.
• DHS bought an 833,280-square-foot warehouse in Salt Lake City for $145.4 million without notifying city or state leaders.
• The city of Salt Lake City has moved to cap water use at the warehouse.
• The owner of another Salt Lake City warehouse announced plans not to sell or lease to the federal government.
• Jim Pattison Developments announced it would not proceed with a planned sale of a warehouse in Richmond, Virginia, after boycott threats.
summary: A look at some of the locations: Local officials were told nothing before ICE purchased a 418,000-square-foot (38,833-square-meter) warehouse in the Phoenix suburb of Surprise for $70 million, the state’s top prosecutor, Kris Mayes, said in a letter to former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. Documents later provided by ICE said the Department of Homeland Security plans a processing site with an average daily capacity of 1,000 to 1,500, and a contract worth at least $313.4 million was awarded to transform it.
